answer: DeepWalk is often described as using random walks plus a skip-gram objective, but on citation networks such as DBLP(PaperCitation) the graph structure is usually sparse and highly skewed, so weighted edges and matrix factorization are used to better preserve local link strength. Weighted edges let the model treat some citations or co-occurrences as stronger than others, which helps encode first-order proximity: directly connected nodes should have similar embeddings, and stronger connections should pull embeddings closer. Matrix factorization is then used as an efficient way to approximate the proximity matrix implied by the graph, turning the problem into learning low-dimensional vectors whose dot products reproduce observed edge weights or co-occurrence statistics. In short, the combination helps DeepWalk capture immediate neighborhood similarity more faithfully than an unweighted random-walk view alone, especially in citation graphs where direct citation relationships are the main signal.
